question: Someone says an invisible, floating, heatless dragon lives in their garage. Why should you not believe it?
answer: Sagan's point: every test you propose, flour on the floor, an infrared camera, paint, meets a new reason it cannot work. A claim that no possible observation could show false tells you nothing about the world. The burden is on whoever makes it, not on you to disprove it.
move: If nothing could ever prove a claim wrong, it says nothing.
simply: If a friend says there's a dragon you can't see, hear, touch or measure in any way, then there's no difference between that dragon and no dragon at all.
why: Many claims, from miracle cures to conspiracy theories, protect themselves the same way. Asking 'what would show this is false?' sorts them in seconds.
reference: Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (Random House, 1995), ch. 10
